claims.text: A homogenized, primarily single-phase high-entropy alloy is the intended initial material state.
The intervention is addition of 2–5 at.% of a dopant, potentially a refractory element.
The added dopant will preferentially segregate to grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary dopant segregation will reduce grain-boundary mobility.
Grain-boundary dopant segregation will inhibit diffusion-controlled creep mechanisms.
Reduced grain-boundary mobility will reduce grain-boundary sliding at high temperature.
Dopant-induced grain-boundary stabilization will reduce diffusion at high temperature.
Reduced grain-boundary sliding and diffusion will delay high-temperature deformation.
The doped alloy will have a significantly lower creep rate than the undoped alloy under identical test conditions.
The doped alloy will have significantly greater high-temperature yield strength than the undoped alloy under identical test conditions.
The proposed improvement is expected between 800°C and 1000°C under mechanical load in an oxidizing environment.
The hypothesis applies to high-entropy alloys having phase compositions similar to that of the baseline alloy.
The proposed benefit may fail when severe oxidation or another environmental degradation mechanism dominates.
The proposed mechanism is an extrapolation of principles from conventional alloys to high-entropy alloys.
A controlled comparison at 850°C in an oxidizing atmosphere under constant load can test the proposed property improvements and grain-boundary segregation.
